open-question.question: Does an extension release make a commit of its own, and under which subject, given that `/release-plugin` recognises its own interrupted run by a `HEAD` subject of exactly `Release: <VERSION>`?
open-question.recommendation: The version-source decision has the skill write the version itself, which closes the no-commit option; of the rest, a marker of its own keeps every reader of `Release:`, exact or prefix, on plugin releases with `/release-plugin` untouched, and gives the skill the same one-line resumption test.
open-question.alternative: The release skill makes one commit of its own, holding only what the release writes into the tree (the extension's version slots and any changelog entry), under a new marker that does not open with `Release:`, `Extension-release: <VERSION>` with the version as the whole descriptor. The skill recognises its own interrupted run by a `HEAD` subject of exactly that string, as `/release-plugin` recognises its own, and `/release-plugin` is left untouched. The two release kinds are told apart by the marker alone: no exact or prefix match on `Release:` can reach an extension release, a version number shared by the plugin and the extension never makes the two subjects equal, and each skill keeps the same one-line resumption test. A new marker joins the workflow's subject vocabulary and must be documented beside `Release:`, and a reader looking for every release in the log needs two patterns rather than one.

The extension's release skill makes no commit and writes nothing to the tree: it builds and publishes the version the manifest already holds, and whatever a release needs in the repository (a version bump in `gurita-vscode/package.json` and `package-lock.json`, any changelog entry) is committed beforehand by hand under ordinary subjects. No release marker is introduced, `/release-plugin` is left untouched, and the skill does not recognise an interrupted run from `HEAD`'s subject. No subject the extension writes can ever be read by `/release-plugin` as its own `Release: <VERSION>`, because no extension release commit exists; the skill stays a pure build-and-publish step with no commit logic and no new marker for any reader to learn. Viable only if the sibling questions on the version source and the extension changelog leave the skill nothing to write; the log then records no point at which a version was released, and the skill must detect a resumed run some other way, for instance by querying the registries, so the history alone cannot say which commit any published version was built from.

The release skill makes one commit of its own, holding only what the release writes into the tree, under the existing `Release:` marker with a descriptor naming the extension ahead of the version, for example `Release: gurita-vscode <VERSION>`. The skill recognises its own interrupted run by an exact `HEAD` subject of that form; `/release-plugin`'s exact test for `Release: <VERSION>` is left untouched and cannot match it, since the descriptor differs. Every release of either artifact sits under one marker, so one `^Release:` search lists them all while each subject still names what was released, and `/release-plugin`'s exact-match resumption check is unaffected without any edit. Any present or future reader keyed on the `Release:` prefix rather than the exact subject (a log filter, release-note composition reading the range's subjects) would take an extension release for a plugin one, so the safety rests on every such reader matching exactly and on the descriptor being parsed to tell the two apart.

The release skill makes one commit of its own under the plugin's exact form, `Release: <VERSION>` with the extension's version, and `/release-plugin`'s resumption detection is changed so that a matching subject counts only when that commit also changed the root `VERSION` (or another plugin-only file) to `<VERSION>`; the extension skill applies the mirror test on `gurita-vscode/package.json`. One uniform release subject for the whole repository, with each skill's resumption test keyed on what the commit actually changed rather than on its wording alone. It edits `/release-plugin`, a working release path, to defend against a collision another choice would never create, and the subject alone no longer says which artifact a release commit released, so a plugin and an extension release of the same version number produce identical subjects in the log.

open-question.question: Does an extension release create a GitHub release in `uHappyLogic/gurita`, with or without the VSIX attached, or do the two registries alone carry it?
open-question.recommendation: The tracked changelog already puts each version's notes on both listings and the release tag marks its commit, so a GitHub release would add only a page to keep off Latest and one more place for a cut-off run to resume, while the releases page, the root badge, and the root changelog go on meaning the plugin with nothing to guard.
open-question.alternative: An extension release creates no GitHub release in `uHappyLogic/gurita`, or anywhere else on GitHub. It publishes the package to the Visual Studio Marketplace and to Open VSX only, and the repository's releases page goes on holding plugin releases alone. The repository's releases page, the root README's `Latest Release` badge and its `releases/latest` link, and the root `CHANGELOG.md`'s rule that each entry is the notes of that version's GitHub release all keep meaning the plugin with nothing to guard. The release skill also has one fewer public step to check and resume when a run is cut off partway. Nowhere on GitHub records an extension release. Its notes reach a reader only through the listings, and only as far as whatever changelog the package carries (a sibling's call). There is also no published VSIX outside the two registries, so anyone whose editor reads neither one, or who wants to pin a version and install it by hand with `code --install-extension`, has to build it from the checkout.

An extension release also creates a GitHub release in `uHappyLogic/gurita`. It carries the release's notes and no attached file, and it is created as not latest (`gh release create … --latest=false`), so the plugin's newest release stays the one GitHub marks as Latest. Each extension version gets a dated, linkable notes page in the repository's own release history, next to the plugin's. It costs one more check-then-do `gh` step of the kind `/release-plugin` already runs, with no binary to keep in step with what the registries hold. The page has nothing to install, so a reader has to go to a listing anyway. Extension and plugin releases get mixed together in one list. Every run must keep the release off Latest, or the root README's badge and `releases/latest` link quietly switch to the extension. A GitHub release also stands on a tag, so whether this works depends on the tag question a sibling owns, and the half-published re-run (also a sibling's) gets a third place it has to check.

An extension release also creates a GitHub release in `uHappyLogic/gurita`. It carries the release's notes and has the very VSIX that was published to both registries attached as an asset. It is created as not latest (`gh release create … --latest=false`), so the plugin's newest release stays the one GitHub marks as Latest. Every published version can be downloaded from GitHub as the exact package both registries hold. That serves an editor that reads neither registry, an offline or pinned install by hand through the `code --install-extension` call the README documents today, and anyone checking what a registry served. It also keeps a copy of each version that does not depend on either registry. The run has one more public artifact to get right. The file it uploads must be the same bytes it published, so it has to build once and publish from that one file. A re-run has to check the asset by name as well as the release, since an asset can be replaced even though a registry version cannot. It carries every cost of the notes-only release too: the mixed release list, keeping it off Latest on every run, and depending on the tag question and the half-published re-run, both owned by siblings.

open-question.question: Which conditions must hold before the extension's release skill changes or publishes anything, for example a clean tracked tree, `main` not behind `origin/main`, the extension's tests and the runner's tests passing, a package that builds, and tokens both registries still accept?
open-question.applied-principle: Check tier claims against the live environment

recommendation.option: Full gate with live token check

open-question.recommendation: With both tokens in the maintainer's shell, `vsce verify-pat` and `ovsx verify-pat` can ask each registry before anything is written, which catches the expired or mis-scoped token, the likeliest way to end with one registry holding the version; the test and build stops carry `/release-plugin`'s gate-before-write rule over without a hand-kept list of package contents.

alternative.id: Full gate with live token check

open-question.alternative: Before it writes or publishes anything, the skill runs a fixed set of hard stops, each ending the run with nothing changed and the reason reported, never waived. Repository state: the tracked tree is clean, `HEAD` is on `main`, `main` is not behind `origin/main` after a fetch, and no untracked file stands under the extension's source paths outside its git-ignored build directories. Toolchain: Node 22 answers through nvm, `npm ci` installs the pinned dependencies, and `vsce` and the Open VSX publishing tool both resolve. Tests: the extension's `node:test` suite (`npm test`) and the runner's `runner_tests/` pass. Build: `npm run package` builds the VSIX into the ignored `dist/`. Tokens: each registry's token is checked live against that registry for the `uhappylogic` publisher or namespace (the verify-token commands both publishing tools offer), which also confirms the publisher and the namespace exist. Every failure a publish could meet, a stale or dirty tree, a broken build, failing tests, and an expired, wrongly scoped, or missing token or publisher, is caught before either registry is touched, so a release can no longer stop with one registry holding the version and the other not because of anything checkable in advance; it carries `/release-plugin`'s gate-before-write rule over to the extension. The slowest and most involved pre-flight: it needs network access to both registries and sends both tokens before publishing, adds the Open VSX publishing tool as something the run must find, and its token step's form depends on where the tokens are kept and where the skill runs, an axis the publish-site question owns; on a workflow run the clean-tree and behind-origin checks become largely moot.

The same repository-state, toolchain, test, and build stops as the full gate, all hard stops, but the tokens are checked only for being present and readable where the skill reads them (set and non-empty), with no query to either registry before publishing. Catches the common misconfiguration, a token never set or not visible to the run, without any network call to the registries or any use of a token before the publish itself, and needs no verify command from either publishing tool. An expired, revoked, or wrongly scoped token, or a publisher or namespace that does not exist, surfaces only at publish time, possibly after the first registry already accepted the version, which leaves exactly the half-published state a sibling question has to handle; where the tokens live, and so what "present" means, is owned by the publish-site question.

alternative.id: Full gate plus whole suite and package inspection

open-question.alternative: Everything the full gate with live token check runs, and two further hard stops: the repository's whole Python suite at both interpreters (`uv run pytest` and the 3.9 floor run), which also covers the missions tool the package bundles, and an inspection of the built VSIX's file list and manifest, stopping when it holds anything under `mission_*`, sources, or tests, or lacks the listing icon, the listing README, the license, or the bundled files. Also guards what the package carries rather than only that it builds: a `.vscodeignore` slip shipping mission files or sources, or a listing asset missing from the package, is stopped before it becomes a public, unremovable version, and the bundled missions tool is tested in the same run. The longest run, repeating checks the plugin's own release and CI already make, and the content inspection is a second list of expected files that must be kept in step with `.vscodeignore` and the listing assets by hand; whether the bundled sources must be those of a released plugin version is a separate question this inspection does not settle.

The skill stops before writing anything only on repository state (clean tracked tree, `HEAD` on `main`, not behind `origin/main`, no untracked file under the extension's sources) and on a live check of both registries' tokens; it runs no tests and makes no package build in the pre-flight, the package being built only by the publish step itself. A short, fast pre-flight that still blocks the two failures most likely to produce an unreproducible or half-published release, while relying on every task of the missions that changed the extension having already verified its tests and build before its commit. A failing test or a broken package from a hand commit or a dependency drift is found only when the publish step builds, or not at all when the build succeeds but the code is wrong, and a published version cannot be republished; the token step's form again depends on the publish-site question.

The skill has no gate of its own: it builds and publishes directly, and a failure of the build, a publishing tool, or a registry stops it with that tool's own message; the conditions the question lists are left to the maintainer to see to before invoking it. The simplest skill to write and keep: nothing duplicates what the publishing tools already refuse, and the run is as short as publishing allows. Nothing stops a release from a dirty, outdated, or wrong-branch tree, a failing test suite ships, and a token or publisher problem on the second registry is found only after the first accepted the version, leaving a half-published release; it also breaks with `/release-plugin`'s rule that every gate passes before anything is changed or published.

open-question.question: A version a registry has accepted cannot be published to it again. What does a re-run of the extension's release skill with the same version do after one of the two registries accepted that version and the other did not?
open-question.applied-principle: Check tier claims against the live environment
open-question.recommendation: The same two publish commands serve the first run and every re-run with no query and no branch, in line with the recorded choice to observe nothing on the registries; the skip rests on each registry's own refusal, which both tools turn into a printed skip line and a successful exit, so a re-run cannot trip over a read side lagging behind a version already accepted.
open-question.alternative: The re-run asks no registry anything. It runs both publishes again, each with the `--skip-duplicate` flag that the pinned `vsce` 4.1.1 offers ("Fail silently if version already exists on the marketplace") and that `ovsx publish` also offers. The registry that already holds the version turns its publish into a silent success, and the other one receives the version from a package rebuilt from the state the version was released from. Of all the ways to resume, this one adds the least to the skill: the same two publish commands serve the first run and every re-run, with no query code and no branch. The skill cannot tell a duplicate it skipped from a fresh publish, so its report cannot say which registry the re-run actually published to. It also relies on both CLIs keeping the flag's behaviour across upgrades, and a skipped duplicate is never checked against the package that was accepted.

Before each publish, the re-run asks the registry whether it already holds the version (the Marketplace through `vsce show`, Open VSX through its public REST query on `uhappylogic/gurita-vscode/<version>`). It skips the registry that does and publishes only to the one that does not, from a package rebuilt from the state the version was released from, then goes on to whatever later release steps remain. This is the check-then-do resumption `/release-plugin` already uses for each of its publish steps. A re-run with the same version finishes the release exactly where it stopped, with one rule, query first and skip when done, shared with the plugin's release skill, and the skill can tell the maintainer which registry it skipped and which it published to. It needs a query per registry written into the skill and depends on each registry's read side reporting a version soon after the version is accepted. The rebuilt package matches the one already accepted only if the rebuild starts from the same repository state, which leans on how the release records that state (the sibling questions on the release commit and the tag).

As in the query-and-resume option, the re-run queries each registry and publishes only to the one missing the version. What it publishes is not a rebuild but the very VSIX file the first run built and published to the registry that accepted it. That file is kept where the re-run can find it under the version's name, for example under `dist/` on the publishing machine or as a release asset. Both registries are guaranteed to carry the same bytes for the version, whatever happened to the checkout, its bundled sources, or the toolchain between the two runs. The release has to keep a built artifact the repository has so far never kept (`dist/` is git-ignored and the VSIX is never committed), and a re-run whose retained file is gone has nothing to publish. Whether a file survives between runs depends on the sibling question of where the release publishes from, since a workflow run's workspace does not outlive it.

The re-run queries both registries. When exactly one holds the version, it publishes nothing and stops, printing which registry is missing the version and the exact `vsce publish` or `ovsx publish` command the maintainer runs on the package to finish. This follows the way `/release-plugin` prints the commands for a missing repository or token and exits without running them. The skill never publishes in a state it did not start from cleanly, so the irreversible second publish is a deliberate act by the maintainer, and the skill needs no resume path past the publish steps. A transient failure, such as a network error or a registry outage, costs the maintainer a hand step outside the skill, done with a CLI and a token they must have at hand. Any release steps that follow the publishes are left for the maintainer to finish by hand or by a further re-run.

The skill has no logic for a half-published version. A re-run with the same version runs its steps as on a first run, the registry that already holds the version refuses the publish, and the skill stops on that registry's error. Completing the release on the other registry is left wholly to the maintainer, who publishes by hand. Nothing is added to the skill for a case that may never arise once its pre-flight checks pass, and the registry's own refusal keeps the accepted version from being overwritten. The one failure the question names ends in a stop with no guidance. A re-run, the natural response, can never succeed for that version, so the maintainer has to work out the missing publish alone. How often this happens depends on the sibling question of which pre-flight checks run first (tokens both registries still accept among them).

Once either registry holds a version, a re-run with that version refuses, naming the registry that holds it. The release is completed by running the skill with the next version, which goes to both registries, and the half-published version stays on the one registry that accepted it. No version is ever published in two separate runs, so the two registries never carry bytes for one version that were built at different times, and the skill needs only one "version already taken" check. The registries' version histories diverge for good, with a version that exists on only one of them. Every half-published attempt also burns a version number and repeats the whole release, version write, notes, and any commit or tag included. How much of that repeats depends on the sibling questions of where the version comes from and whether the release commits and tags.

open-question.question: Does the extension's release skill pause for the maintainer's confirmation before it publishes, as `/release-plugin` pauses once before anything public, or run through unattended once its checks pass?
open-question.recommendation: Publishing from the maintainer's machine, as recorded, closes the workflow-approval option; one pause at the line between undoable local work and two registries that never take a version twice is the gate `/release-plugin` already has and its maintainer already knows, with the notes shown in full and revisable before they are public.
open-question.alternative: The skill pauses exactly once, on every run, after its pre-flight checks and all local work and before anything public (the first registry upload, and any push, tag, or GitHub release the release makes). The pause shows the version about to be published and the release notes in full, verbatim, as they will be published. It accepts three answers, as `/release-plugin`'s step 7 does: an explicit publish proceeds, a stated revision of the notes is applied and the version and notes are shown again, and anything else stops with nothing public done. The gate is never skipped and no flag bypasses it. It mirrors the one pause `/release-plugin` already has and its maintainer already knows, placed at the one point where everything before is undoable and everything after is permanent (a version a registry has accepted cannot be published to it again), so the maintainer vetoes or fixes the public text before it is out. The run cannot complete unattended or in a headless chain. What the pause shows, and whether a revision can be applied in place, depends on whether the release composes notes and records them in a commit of its own, axes the Release notes source, Extension changelog, and Release commit subject questions own.

alternative.id: Single pause on the built package

open-question.alternative: The skill pauses exactly once, on every run, after the VSIX has been built and before anything public. The pause shows the version, the release notes where the release has any, and the built package itself: its path, size, and file list, which is what both listings will show (the README, the icon, the manifest's listing metadata). It invites the maintainer to install that VSIX into VS Code by hand (`code --install-extension` on its path) and try it before answering. An explicit publish proceeds and anything else stops with nothing public done. The gate is never skipped and no flag bypasses it. It catches a defect in the package itself, such as a README that renders wrongly, a missing bundled file, or a wrong icon, on the exact artifact the registries will receive and before either can accept a version that can never be published again. It is the longest pause, adding a hand install and a try to every release, including routine ones where the package changed little, and the file list it shows is long (37 files today) for a maintainer to read on each run.

The skill pauses twice on every run: once before it publishes to the first registry, showing the version and the notes, and once more after the first registry has accepted the version and before it publishes to the second, inviting the maintainer to look at the first listing as it now stands. An explicit publish at each pause proceeds; anything else stops, the second time with one registry carrying the version and the other not. Neither pause is skipped. A defect that shows only on a live listing (how the README, icon, or metadata render on the registry's page) stops the release before it reaches the second registry. It doubles the prompts, and a stop at the second pause leaves a half-published release by the maintainer's own choice, a state whose re-run behaviour the Half-published release question owns, while the first registry's version stays published and unrepairable anyway.

The skill pauses once, before anything public, showing the version and the notes, only when the extension is not yet listed on the registries, which it learns by querying them; once the extension is live on both, every later release runs through unattended once its pre-flight checks pass. No flag changes either behaviour. It puts the human check where the novelty is, the first appearance of the publisher, the listing name, and its metadata, which cannot be renamed or reused once wrong, while routine releases afterwards need no attendance. Every later release publishes a version and notes that no one reviewed before they became permanent, and the skill gains a registry query and a branch on its result, a second behaviour to maintain for what is a single run (the mission's own first publication).

The skill pauses once by default, before anything public, showing the version and the notes, with explicit publish proceeding and anything else stopping. A flag given on the invocation (for example `--yes`) skips the pause, so the run goes through unattended once its pre-flight checks pass. The maintainer reviews by default, yet a scripted or headless release is possible without editing the skill. It adds a second mode to a maintainer-only skill run by one person, and departs from `/release-plugin`, whose pause is never skipped; a flag habitually given turns the gate into no gate, with an irreversible publication behind it.

The skill never pauses: the maintainer's invocation is the consent, and once its pre-flight checks pass it publishes to both registries unattended. Whatever it shows of the version and the notes it prints as it goes, after the fact. It is the simplest skill and the fastest run, it completes in a headless chain with nothing to answer, and the version to release is already stated by the maintainer at invocation wherever the skill takes it as an argument. Nothing the run composes or builds, notes, listing text, or package, is seen before it becomes permanent on two registries that never accept the same version twice, so a mistake costs a new version to correct. How much the invocation already says depends on whether the version is given as an argument, an axis the Version source at release question owns.

The skill itself never pauses: it starts the publishing workflow once its checks pass, and the workflow's publish job runs under a GitHub Actions environment with the maintainer as its required reviewer, so publication waits until the maintainer approves the job on GitHub, where the run's version and inputs are shown; a rejected or unapproved job publishes nothing. The approval is recorded on GitHub beside the run that published, and it holds even when the workflow is started from somewhere other than the skill, so no path publishes unapproved. It exists only if the release publishes from a GitHub Actions workflow rather than from the maintainer's machine, an axis the Publish site and tokens question owns, and it adds an environment and its protection rule to the repository's settings, which nothing in the tree records or checks.

open-question.question: The published package's `engines.vscode` floor is set to the oldest VS Code base among the Open VSX forks the extension means to reach, but nothing recorded names those forks. Which editors that read Open VSX does the extension mean to reach, for example VSCodium, Cursor, Windsurf, or Antigravity?
open-question.applied-principle: Check tier claims against the live environment
open-question.recommendation: All four read Open VSX and are where a Claude Code, Codex, or Antigravity user is most likely to work, so naming them is what makes the Open VSX listing reach the people the goal publishes it for; the list stays short enough to look each base up when the floor is set, and the compile against the re-pinned typings shows at once whether the lower floor costs an API.
open-question.alternative: The extension means to reach the four editors the question names, VSCodium, Cursor, Windsurf, and Antigravity: the widely used editors that read Open VSX and carry an agent of their own. The floor is the oldest of their four bases, looked up when the change is made, likely Cursor's or Windsurf's, and `@types/vscode` is re-pinned to the newest typings not above it. Other Open VSX readers (Kiro, Trae, Theia, code-server, Gitpod) are not named and are reached only where their base meets that floor. It covers the editors that hold nearly all of the Open VSX audience a Claude Code, Codex, or Antigravity user is likely to run, so the Open VSX listing reaches the people the goal publishes it for, and the target list stays short and nameable. The floor drops furthest of the named-list options, to whichever of the four lags most. That can mean typings many minor versions older than the 1.140.0 the code compiles against today, so an API the code uses may turn out to be missing and need a rewrite, and with no install in any fork, a fork's own deviations from upstream go unseen.

The extension means to reach VSCodium alone among the editors that read Open VSX. VSCodium is rebuilt from each upstream VS Code release, so the oldest base in the set is VSCodium's current release, looked up when the change is made, and `engines.vscode` stays at or barely below today's `^1.143.0`, with `@types/vscode` re-pinned only if that release is below 1.140. Cursor, Windsurf, Antigravity, and every other fork are named nowhere as targets: they get the extension wherever their own base already meets the floor, and nothing is lowered for them. Almost nothing changes. The floor stays close to the editor the extension was built and tested in, the re-pin of `@types/vscode` is small or not needed, and the package never claims to support an editor whose base lags well behind upstream VS Code. The forks that lag upstream by several minor versions, Cursor, Windsurf, and Antigravity among them, would refuse to install the extension until they catch up. That leaves out the forks most of the Open VSX audience uses, Antigravity included, whose agent `agy` is one of the plugin's three harnesses, so the Open VSX publication would reach little more than VSCodium users.

The extension means to reach VSCodium and Antigravity, the editor of `agy`, one of the three harnesses whose installed plugin copies the extension's harness check looks up. The floor is the older of the two bases, in practice Antigravity's, looked up when the change is made, and `@types/vscode` is re-pinned to the newest typings not above it. Cursor, Windsurf, and the other forks are not targets and are reached only where their base meets that floor. The target set follows the plugin's own harness set. An Antigravity user running the plugin's `agy` harness can install the extension in the same editor, and the floor drops only as far as that one lagging fork needs. Cursor and Windsurf are left to chance: if their base is older than Antigravity's, they refuse the install, though their users are as likely as anyone to run Claude Code or Codex beside them. Because the recorded listing-verification decision installs the extension in no editor, the floor is also never tried in Antigravity itself.

alternative.id: Every Open VSX reader the API allows

open-question.alternative: No fork list is named. The extension means to reach every editor that reads Open VSX, VSCodium, Cursor, Windsurf, Antigravity, Kiro, Trae, Theia, code-server, and Gitpod included, as far as its present API use allows. The floor is the oldest VS Code version whose API covers what the code uses now (webview panels and their serializer, a tree view, terminals with `isTransient` and `exitStatus`, `ThemeIcon`, and file-system watchers), found by compiling against successively older typings, and `@types/vscode` is pinned to that version. Any fork whose base meets the floor is in the set without being named. It gives the widest reach the code allows without being changed, since the APIs it uses are long-standing, and the target set never has to be revisited when a fork moves its base or a new fork appears. The floor follows from the code rather than from a survey of fork versions that goes stale. Reading the recorded engine-floor decision as a floor set by API use rather than by named forks stretches its wording. Very old typings also lose the later API refinements the code silently relies on, which only a compile shows, and editors whose extension host deviates most from VS Code (Theia, browser-hosted code-server) are claimed by the floor while nothing ever checks that the runner and the terminals work in them.

open-question.question: The extension's release skill runs `ovsx publish`, but `ovsx` is no dependency of the extension and is installed nowhere, while `@vscode/vsce` is a dev dependency pinned to an exact version. How does a release get the `ovsx` tool: as a dev dependency of `gurita-vscode/` pinned like `vsce`, fetched when the release runs, or installed by the maintainer outside the repository?
open-question.applied-principle: Check tier claims against the live environment
open-question.recommendation: Both publishing tools then come from one lockfile, fixed with their transitive dependencies by integrity hash before they run in a shell holding both tokens, and the skill needs no install step or version check of its own; a dry run of the lockfile with `ovsx` 1.4.0, which asks for `@vscode/vsce` `^4.0.0`, kept the single pinned 4.1.1 copy.
open-question.alternative: Source: the extension's own Node project. `ovsx` is added to `devDependencies` in `gurita-vscode/package.json` at an exact version, beside `@vscode/vsce` 4.1.1, and recorded in `package-lock.json`, so `npm ci` in `gurita-vscode/` installs it into `node_modules/`. Pin: exact, held by the manifest and the lockfile.
